body.en: Advanced ACT Math includes combinations, permutations, compound probability, and normal distribution concepts.
How many 3-letter arrangements (order matters) can be made from the word MATH? \[ _4P_3=\frac{4!}{1!}=24. \]

Fundamental counting principle: \(m \times n\) ways for two independent events. Expected value: \(E(X) = \sum x_i P(x_i)\). Standard normal: \(z = \dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\); about 68% of data within \(1\sigma\), 95% within \(2\sigma\), 99.7% within \(3\sigma\).

A game pays $8 if you roll a 6 on a fair die, and you lose $2 otherwise. What is the expected gain per roll?

\(E = 8 \cdot \dfrac{1}{6} + (-2) \cdot \dfrac{5}{6} = \dfrac{8-10}{6} = -\dfrac{2}{6} \approx -\$0.33\).

The game is unfair — you lose on average 33 cents per roll.

label.en: ▲ ACT Math 2 Traps & Pitfalls — Probability, Counting & Normal Curves

body.en:
• Permutations vs. Combinations: Ask: 'Does order matter?' If order matters (ranking, electing distinct officers, line arrangements), use permutations \(_nP_r\). If group membership is all that counts (committees, picking toppings, drawing cards), use combinations \(\binom{n}{r}\).
  • The Complement Shortcut for 'At Least One': Questions asking for the probability of 'at least one' of an event occurring are almost always solved fastest using the complement: \(P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - P(\text{none})\).
  • Signs in Expected Value: Losses, entry fees, or payouts must include their respective positive or negative signs in \(E = \sum x_i P(x_i)\). If a ticket costs \(\$5\) with a prize of \(\$20\), the net gain when winning is \(+\$15\), not \(\$20\).
  • Empirical Rule Sub-Intervals: Between the mean and \(+1\sigma\) lies \(34\%\); between \(+1\sigma\) and \(+2\sigma\) lies \(13.5\%\); between \(+2\sigma\) and \(+3\sigma\) lies \(2.35\%\); and above \(+3\sigma\) lies approximately \(0.15\%\).

question.en: In a class of 30, 18 play football (F), 14 play basketball (B), and 6 play both. How many play neither sport?

A school committee of 4 members is to be selected from a club consisting of 6 juniors and 5 seniors. (a) In how many total ways can the 4 members be selected? (b) In how many ways can the committee be formed if it must contain exactly 2 juniors and 2 seniors?

solution.en:
(a) Unrestricted selection: Total students \(= 6 + 5 = 11\). Choosing 4 where order does not matter: \[ \binom{11}{4} = \dfrac{11 \times 10 \times 9 \times 8}{4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1} = 11 \times 10 \times 3 = 330 \text{ ways}. \]

(b) Exactly 2 juniors and 2 seniors: Select 2 juniors from 6, AND 2 seniors from 5: \[ \binom{6}{2} \times \binom{5}{2} = \left( \dfrac{6 \times 5}{2} \right) \times \left( \dfrac{5 \times 4}{2} \right) = 15 \times 10 = 150 \text{ ways}. \]
